articles.title: Prime Intellect acquires Moondream, a vision AI startup founded in Seattle by AWS vets
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Prime Intellect , a San Francisco-based AI cloud company valued at $1 billion, has acquired Moondream , a startup founded in Seattle by Amazon Web Services veterans that makes small, open-source AI models for understanding images.

Terms weren’t disclosed. Moondream has fewer than 10 employees, according to The Information , which first reported the deal Tuesday. Prime Intellect announced the acquisition later in the day in a blog post and on X .

Moondream emerged in 2024 with a $4.5 million pre-seed round from Felicis, Microsoft’s M12 GitHub Fund and Seattle-based Ascend. Its original model was small enough to run on phones and other devices.

The startup’s co-founders Jay Allen and Vik Korrapati are joining Prime Intellect to lead its inference work — running AI models after they’re trained — and to expand its efforts in vision and computer-using AI agents, the company said.
Prime Intellect is largely buying Moondream for its team’s skill at making models run faster, CEO Vincent Weisser said, according to The Information.

Moondream built Photon , an inference engine that compiles each AI model into a single program on the GPU, known as a megakernel, reducing the chip’s idle time between tasks. Engineers have historically written megakernels by hand, the report said.

Prime Intellect is one of a wave of “neoclouds” that provide computing power for AI developers and help them run open-source models. It raised $130 million in a Series A round led by Radical Ventures in July and said at the time that it had passed $100 million in annualized revenue.
Moondream was one of Prime Intellect’s earliest customers, according to the blog post.

Prime Intellect will keep using the Moondream name for small, efficient AI models that handle images and other types of data. Its latest model, Moondream 3.1, is available through Prime Intellect’s inference service, and Moondream Cloud customers will receive credits on Prime Intellect’s platform.
Korrapati, Moondream’s CTO, spent nine years at AWS. Allen, its CEO, spent seven years at AWS and previously worked at Porch, Zynga and Microsoft.

Moondream said earlier this year that it was moving to San Francisco . Korrapati announced the move in January in an online post calling AI “the biggest platform shift we’re going to see in our working lives.” Allen’s LinkedIn profile still lists him in Seattle.

articles.title: Tech Moves: Brinc Drones, Fred Hutch, Acumatica, Convera add to C-suites; LinkedIn director departs
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: — Brinc Drones , the Seattle-based maker of 911 response drones, has named Joe Levy chief revenue officer. Levy joins from Peregrine, a public safety data platform, and early in his career was a drill sergeant and combat engineer for the U.S. Army Reserve.
Levy praised the Brinc team, saying, “They’re passionate about what they do with a vision that will change the public safety landscape. I’m grateful to join them and help scale what they’ve built.”

Brinc announced a $125 million funding round in July, bringing its total raised to more than $280 million. The startup is hiring for numerous roles and is No. 6 on the GeekWire 200 , a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.
— Seattle-based Fred Hutch Cancer Center has appointed Jessie Minton vice president and chief digital and information officer, a new position that brings the roles together.

Former Chief Data Officer Jeff Leek stepped down and is now a professor in the Fred Hutch Public Health Sciences Division and CEO of Synthesize Bio, a startup he co-founded in 2023. Last month, Fred Hutch announced Shawn Stapleton as VP and chief AI and innovation officer, another new role.

Minton joins from Washington University in St. Louis where she has been vice chancellor for technology and chief information officer since 2022. She was previously VP and CIO at the University of Oregon.

Fred Hutch praised Minton’s track record “of modernizing complex technology organizations, strengthening cybersecurity, governing large-scale Epic environments and aligning technology strategy with clinical, research and academic priorities.” The new role is effective Dec. 7.

— Jason (JJ) James has been named chief information officer of Acumatica , the Bellevue, Wash.-based enterprise software giant that was acquired last year by Vista Equity Partners. James has more than 25 years in technology leadership and was previously CIO at companies including Aptos Retail, Net Health and Optima Healthcare Solutions.

“My focus is putting AI to work across Acumatica while keeping security at the core, so we can move fast without compromising the trust our expanding community of customers, partners and developers places in us,” James said in a statement.

— Seattle tech leader Andrew Bennett has joined San Francisco-based Motive as chief marketing officer. Bennett was with Smartsheet for a decade, leaving as CMO in 2024. He is also a limited partner with the investment firm Stage 2 Capital.
Motive provides software, hardware and AI-powered tools to help businesses manage physical fleets of vehicles and heavy equipment.
— Steven Chen has left LinkedIn, where he served as director and head of corporate legal and sustainability, to become a senior director at Rubrik .

— Seattle-based LevelTen Energy , a startup facilitating the deployment of clean energy projects, has appointed John Barrow as director of a new initiative enabling the purchase and sale of data center projects under development.
Barrow joins from CyrusOne, a global data center developer and operator, and was with CPS Energy for more than 15 years.

“In my career, I’ve had a front-row seat to the data center boom,” Barrow said. Participants are struggling to quickly secure locations and energy, he said, adding that LevelTen “can solve those problems for industry participants at scale.”

— Certivo , a Seattle startup building technology to automate supply chain compliance, has named Jeffrey Bornstein to its board. Bornstein was with GE for nearly three decades and served in roles including vice chairman and chief financial officer.

“He has run the numbers for some of the most complex industrial supply chains in the world while regulators checked every one of them,” said Certivo CEO Kunal Chopra. Certivo is No. 194 on the GeekWire 200 .
— Convera , a Seattle-based fintech company helping businesses transfer money across borders, has added to its leadership team. All four will work out of Convera’s other offices.
— Portable Consultants a Redmond, Wash., enterprise telecommunications and data connectivity provider, has named two leaders.
— Reperio Health , a Portland, Ore., startup providing home health screening kits, has named Brad Nations to its board of directors. Nations is CEO and founder of JB Advisory.

— iQmetrix , a Vancouver, B.C.-based company building point-of-sale and retail management software for cell phone and wireless stores, has appointed Beniamin Longodor as VP of global growth. Longodor, who is based in Austria, was previously with NTS Retail.

articles.title: Steve Ballmer’s USAFacts pits Ben Shapiro against Scott Galloway in YouTube debate special
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: USAFacts — the nonpartisan civic data initiative founded by former Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer — is stepping out of its usual spreadsheet-and-report routine and onto the debate stage, launching its first-ever YouTube debate special titled “The American Dream at 250: Data doesn’t argue. They do.”

The 75-minute program pairs conservative commentator and Daily Wire founder Ben Shapiro with progressive author and NYU Stern professor Scott Galloway to hash out escalating cost-of-living pressures and the viability of homeownership — all while tethering their arguments to official government numbers. PBS NewsHour co-anchor Geoff Bennett moderated.

Ballmer steers the effort from the organization’s Fact Desk, leaning into USAFacts’ core mission of grounding national political flashpoints in verified government numbers rather than partisan rhetoric.

“Americans can disagree about the role of government in their lives, but productive debate begins with a shared understanding of the numbers,” USAFacts President Lauren Woodman said in a news release Wednesday, explaining that the project is designed to give the public a common factual baseline to evaluate competing policy choices.
The debate focused on three core economic questions, using federal data as a launching pad:
Capitalism vs. government intervention: The debaters tackled whether free markets or government programs are better equipped to preserve the American Dream and address mounting economic pressures.
The scale of government: They sparred over whether Washington is currently doing too much or too little to intervene in the everyday lives and finances of citizens.

The housing crisis and homeownership: The discussion zeroed in on whether homeownership remains a realistic milestone of the American Dream for younger generations, and whether the government should step in to make housing more attainable.
Founded by Ballmer in 2017 with $10 million of his own money, Bellevue, Wash.-based USAFacts operates like a reporting unit for the public sector, aggregating statistics from over 70 federal sources.

The organization is best known for publishing annual corporate-style “10-K” reports on government revenue and spending, as well as running a data-driven “State of the Union” companion timed to the president’s annual address to Congress.

articles.title: Microsoft’s wild ride: Stock hits new record after a year of ups and downs
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: In less than four months, Microsoft has added roughly half an Amazon to its market value.

The tech giant’s stock has gained about $1.4 trillion in value since early summer, rising from $352.83 on June 25, its lowest close in more than a year, to a record close of $543.45 on Tuesday, giving it a market value just above $4 trillion. The increase over that period is nearly as much as Tesla is worth.

As stock turnarounds go, it’s extraordinary. In January, Microsoft lost $357 billion in a single day , the biggest one-day drop in its history, as investors worried about the company’s AI spending and its reliance on OpenAI. By midsummer, Microsoft was the worst performer this year among the big tech stocks known as the “Magnificent Seven,” according to Morningstar .

The rebound accelerated in late July, when Microsoft reported that Azure, its cloud platform, grew 43% and topped $100 billion in annual revenue. The stock jumped 15.5% the next day. It has mostly kept climbing since, as Microsoft rolled out a revamped Copilot app , a new AI push for Windows and new AI chips .

Microsoft isn’t rising alone. The broader stock market has also been hitting record highs , led by AI stocks. The S&P 500 closed above 7,800 for the first time last week, even as the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield reached its highest level since 2002.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been making a broader pitch along the way. In an essay posted on X in July, he warned that companies relying on outside AI labs “pay for intelligence twice, once with money, and again with something even more valuable,” meaning their own knowledge.
He urged businesses to keep control of that knowledge and avoid tying themselves to any one AI model. Microsoft sells access to models from OpenAI, Anthropic and others, along with its own.

Last weekend, he took up a related theme, calling on X for an “ emergency brake ” on advanced AI models. That means “separating the model from the harness that orchestrates its work,” he wrote. “We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start.”

The message also fits Microsoft’s business interests. As companies use AI models from multiple providers, the advantage could shift to companies like Microsoft that run the cloud and workplace software where businesses keep their data.
Microsoft reports its next quarterly results Oct. 28.

articles.title: Booking Holdings unveils AI travel startup Vayo, based in Seattle, with a planned $100M investment
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Booking Holdings is launching a new Seattle-based travel startup called Vayo , led by serial entrepreneur Mike Fridgen , betting that AI agents built for travel can do a better job of planning and managing trips than general-purpose assistants from the likes of OpenAI and Meta.
The travel giant — parent of Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable — says it plans to invest $100 million in the venture, depending on Vayo’s progress and market conditions.

Vayo, which is opening a waitlist for a free private beta Wednesday, offers AI agents that connect to a user’s inbox to pull in flight, hotel and restaurant confirmations. They then monitor the bookings for price drops, openings at sold-out hotels and other changes.

If a flight is delayed, Vayo flags what that means for the hotel check-in or dinner reservation. It also recommends restaurants and activities based on past trips. Vayo users can make restaurant reservations now, with flight and hotel booking expected in the next few weeks.

The venture is part of a broader effort by Booking Holdings to adapt to the rise of AI agents. Big tech companies and startups are developing general-purpose agents that can plan trips and make bookings, potentially bypassing traditional online travel sites.
The company is pitching Vayo as a personal travel agent “built for trips, not tasks.”

“We are out to build the leading consumer experience in travel — nothing less,” said Fridgen, the company’s CEO and co-founder, who previously led Madrona Venture Labs, the Seattle startup studio, and was CEO of Decide.com, the price-prediction startup acquired by eBay.

Vayo’s website promises neutrality. “Our only agenda is yours,” it says. “Vayo is part of Booking Holdings, but it works for you, not for any one site. If the better room is on the hotel’s own site, or the right stay is on another platform, that’s where Vayo will send you.”

A return to travel : It’s the latest travel venture for Fridgen, who was on the founding team of Expedia’s vacation-package business, co-founded travel startup TripHub, led Alaska Airlines’ digital business and was founding head of product at Farecast, the airfare-prediction startup acquired by Microsoft, after which he led Bing’s travel and shopping search businesses.

Vayo’s CTO and co-founder is Allen Chen , who was previously CTO of Fanatics Collectibles and before that a partner in Boston Consulting Group’s AI practice. A serial entrepreneur himself, Chen co-founded two Seattle software startups, CloudPress and DataBlade, which were acquired by News Corp. and BCG, respectively.

The startup’s head of growth is Ian Fliflet , the former chief growth officer at OfferUp, the mobile marketplace for buying and selling used goods locally. Fridgen said Fliflet helped build OfferUp’s growth from the start and was at the top of his list for the role.
Vayo has about 20 employees, all working in person in downtown Seattle, and has been building the product for about six months. The company’s name is pronounced VAY-oh, as in “vacation.”

For Booking Holdings, the new venture marks a return to Seattle, home to its biggest rival, Expedia Group. Booking.com opened a Seattle office in 2012 and moved it to Bellevue the following year, with plans for as many as 350 jobs. It closed the Bellevue office in 2020, amid the pandemic.

A startup inside a giant: Given the team’s entrepreneurial experience, why build inside a travel giant instead of raising venture capital for an independent startup? For one thing, the arrangement gives Vayo access to Booking Holdings’ travel inventory, infrastructure and capital, while letting the team operate like a startup, Fridgen said in an interview.
Vayo has a unique opportunity to succeed with the backing of the world’s largest online travel company in “a very crowded, very noisy category with a lot of competitors,” he said.
Fridgen was already working on a consumer travel idea when his plans lined up with Booking Holdings’ interest in investing in new ventures. “It was really a meeting of the minds,” he said.

In a footnote in its news release, Booking Holdings said the $100 million investment will be “subject to continued advancement of the product and market conditions.” Fridgen said Vayo’s team will share in the value it creates, without giving details on the ownership structure.

Booking Holdings is also backing Lola , a separate AI startup from Kayak co-founders Steve Hafner and Paul English, which launched last month. “It’s a portfolio approach,” Fridgen said, describing Lola as focused on everyday experiences, such as things to do on a weekend at home, while Vayo is “mile-deep in travel scenarios.”
In a statement, Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel described travel as one of the most complex consumer experiences, with too much of the work still falling on travelers to manage.

Fogel said he’s confident in the Vayo team “and their ability to move with purpose, capitalize on early learnings and adapt at pace as they explore what the next generation of personalization in travel can look like.”

How it works: Vayo is initially targeting frequent leisure travelers who plan trips for family and friends, often in Google Docs, Notion or spreadsheets. That group makes up about 5% of travelers but roughly 30% of travel spending, Fridgen said.

In a demo, Fridgen showed how Vayo built his upcoming trips — to Amsterdam, to Philadelphia to visit his son in college, and to Guatemala for the holidays — within about a minute of connecting to his email. The company says Vayo reads only travel confirmations, not the rest of a user’s inbox.
In this demo video, Vayo plans a trip to Japan, landing a hard-to-get dinner reservation, repricing the flights to save $180 and booking a room at a sold-out hotel when one opens up. (Vayo Video)

Vayo also looks for patterns. For example, it noticed that Fridgen travels to Philadelphia every March, during his son’s sports season, and suggested a mountaineering trip after he climbed Mount Rainier with his daughter this summer.

When the fare dropped on one of his Alaska Airlines flights, Vayo automatically captured the difference as a credit and notified him, Fridgen said. For hotels, it currently prompts users to rebook. During the demo, he reserved a restaurant table through OpenTable without leaving Vayo.

Behind the scenes, Vayo runs numerous AI agents at once, using different models for different jobs. “At any given moment, we have all of these agents working on a user’s behalf,” Chen said. “We are picking the best models that are best suited for those tasks.”
The company has built its own system on top of off-the-shelf AI models, but Chen said the company will probably need its own custom models for some tasks soon.

Vayo connects directly with Booking Holdings brands including Booking.com, Kayak and OpenTable, and has signed a partnership with ticketing platform SeatGeek. Because it pulls travel confirmations from a user’s email, it can also track bookings made anywhere else, including directly with airlines and hotels.
Fridgen said users will be able to book flights and hotels in Vayo in the coming weeks, followed by features for planning trips with travel companions and a native mobile app.

Vayo is free during the private beta. Fridgen said the company hasn’t settled on a business model. A subscription is one possibility as the startup learns which features people are willing to pay for, he said. Fliflet noted that travel also offers traditional revenue from commissions on bookings.

Agents and platforms: Vayo is entering a crowded field of AI travel apps, including trip planners from startups and the big online travel sites. However, Fridgen said he sees general-purpose personal AI agents — such as Meta’s Muse and fast-growing San Francisco startup Instinct — as Vayo’s main competitors.

A growing number of agents have run into resistance from the sites they use. Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from its store last month, and Resy locked out a user whose Instinct agent repeatedly pinged the site for a table.

Vayo is taking a different approach, relying on APIs and direct partnerships with travel companies, Fridgen said. Those direct relationships make the service more reliable for customers and avoid the risk of being blocked, he said.

Fridgen said Vayo wants to work with companies across the industry, not just Booking Holdings brands. The startup doesn’t have a direct relationship with Expedia, but is open to one, he said. “The only way this can live up to its promise as an orchestrator of your travel life that you’ll trust is if it has all the options,” he said, “and that’s what we’re going for.”

articles.title: Humanly acquires CareerArc to connect recruitment marketing with AI hiring
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Bellevue, Wash.-based hiring technology company Humanly has acquired CareerArc to merge its artificial intelligence screening tools with software that helps employers attract job applicants.
The deal announced Wednesday brings together Humanly’s automated chat and interview systems with CareerArc’s social media recruiting and career-site mapping platforms.

The transaction follows an aggressive M&A streak for Humanly, which includes its acquisition of employee engagement platform Anthill earlier this year and a trio of other recruiting tech acquisitions in 2025 — Sprockets, Qualifi, and HourWork.
Founded in 2018, Humanly builds software designed to automate candidate engagement, screening, and interviewing for high-volume employers.

“High volume employers have had to piece together their hiring process with a collection of disconnected tools,” Co-founder and CEO Prem Kumar said in a statement, noting that the deal helps bridge the gap by reaching candidates earlier in the search process.

Founded in 2009, Burbank, Calif.-based CareerArc provides recruitment marketing tools — including social recruiting software and interactive career-site mapping — to help employers reach and convert job seekers.

Its core offerings include HireSocial, a social media recruitment platform designed to automate job postings, and Job Maps, an interactive career-site tool that lets candidates explore open positions visually by location.
Humanly, which is No. 147 on the GeekWire 200 ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups, raised $25 million in Series B funding in April. The startup has raised $52 million to date.
Humanly counts Microsoft, Domino’s, Massage Envy, Worldwide Flight Services, and MGM Resorts and Casinos among its more than 120 customers.
Nine of CareerArc’s 13 employees are joining Humanly, which now employs 50 people.

articles.title: 2026 General Election Endorsements
articles.author: Elections Committee
paras: This midterm election will be a big deal, and not just because Democrats could retake Congress from Republicans and provide a check on Trump’s power at the federal level. A ton of interesting races and measures are also brewing at the local level. Ballots should be arriving in mailboxes by October 16 across Washington state.

It’s imperative that we block megamillionaire Brian Heywood’s latest Eymanesque effort to hijack Washington state’s legislative process through ballot initiative campaigns he and his rich friends bankroll. Their top goal this session seems to be to repeal the millionaires tax, and the benefit to them is obvious. The question is what does lowering taxes on multimillionaires get the rest of us?

As a side quest to their tax the rich repeal battle, Heywood’s campaign also seeks to force schools to turn over kids’ medical records, even if they’re parents are charged with abuse. Plus, they want to inspect your kids’ genitals before they can play sports. This is in the name of the alleged scourge of trans women competing in school sports, but it’s a solution in search of a problem, with a massive amount of harmful side effects. Vote no on all three statewide initiatives from these creepy multimillionaires.

Meanwhile, Washington State’s congressional delegation did not exactly inspire us with confidence that they will be leading the charge to defang Trump, and too few long-time incumbents drew credible challenges. Further down the ticket, however, we see plenty of exciting candidates – some even daring to challenge powerful incumbents and force them to defend how they are adapting to our present political moment.

The progress being made in Olympia stands in stark contrast to intractable federal gridlock on key issues and increasing democratic backsliding. In a productive period from 2023 to 2025, state lawmakers phased out single family zoning in favor of more affordable middle housing, enacted rent stabilization, reformed parking mandates, and barred cities from broadly banning apartments near our biggest transit investments.

The Washington State Legislature is fresh off passing a millionaires tax that will help ease the burden on the working class once it goes into effect in 2029. We were impressed by the broad coalition that advanced the tax, which only hits those who earn more than $1 million in compensation per year, and convinced Governor Bob Ferguson (hardly known for his boldness or backbone) to get behind the effort.

Unfortunately, after queuing up the millionaires’ tax, Ferguson has settled back into his lane of opposing new efforts to tax the rich and focusing the agenda on cuts to state programs. We do not think the work of progressive tax reform is done, and we want to see the state do more to invest in our future, whether expanding public transit, investing in affordable housing, ensuring universal health care, or meeting the state’s paramount duty to ensure the “ample provision for the education of all children.”

Our slate of candidates for the state House and Senate is ready to continue that work, and we’re excited to see what our state can accomplish when it sheds outmoded constraints, like a carcentric approach to infrastructure investments or an instilled fear of taxing the rich.

Oh and did we mention control of the Seattle City Council could also be up for grabs due to a special election in District 5? With centrists still holding a grip on council, progressive legislation continues to face a fraught path forward. Whether Mayor Katie Wilson gets a chance to deliver on campaign promises to make Seattle a more affordable and safe place to live could depend on electing progressive councilmembers, like Nilu Jenks, who [spoiler alert] we enthusiastically endorsed in the D5 race. Read on to see why.

Ballots should be arriving in your mail boxes this week. Washington voters have until 8pm Tuesday, November 3 to return a ballot at a drop box or get it postmarked. Visit the Vote WA portal to register or check your voter information.

The 2026 Elections Committee is led by chairs Forrest Baum and Kelsey Vanhee. Membership includes Tamer Abouzeid, Mike Bollich-Ziegler, Angela Compton, Austin Field, Caitlin Hepworth, Amber Hu, Naomi Lewis, Oliver Moffat, Ryan Packer, Maya Ramakrishnan, Jazmine Smith, and Doug Trumm.

Urbanists will join the long list of groups voting “NO” on Initiative Measure No. IL26-001 (aka the “Parents’ Bill of Rights”).

Sadly, not all kids live in homes that are safe and accepting, and for some vulnerable kids, teachers and school counselors may be the only safe grownups in their lives. Right-wingers have long worked to dismantle public education and attack the educators and staff who work to protect victims of child abuse and LGBTQ+ kids.

Hedge fund manager Brian Heywood is back again trying to trick voters into passing his so-called “Parents’ Bill of Rights” — officially titled “Initiative Measure No. IL26-001.” This badly written initiative would force schools to involuntarily “out” LGBTQ+ kids and strip privacy from child abuse victims.

Voters might be wondering why this scrap of rage bait has risen again. A few years ago, Heywood’s Let’s Go Washington PAC hired signature gatherers to get the first “Parent’s Rights” initiative certified. That original version tried to trick voters into stripping student privacy protections by hiding it within a long list of already existing “Parental Rights”.

But the state legislature defused Heywood’s sneak attack by simply adopting all the duplicative rules while still protecting the privacy of vulnerable children. Now Heywood and his MAGA buddies have once more crawled from under a rock and hired signature gatherers to place their “Parental Rights” initiative back on the ballot.

Urbanists won’t be fooled: this initiative has nothing to do with protecting kids and families. If approved by voters, I-001 would force schools to turn over private records about child abuse victims to their parental abusers. Even parents under criminal investigation for sexual abuse of their child would gain access to private school counseling records.

By requiring schools to disclose highly confidential mental health counseling files to parents, I-001 forces school counselors to “out” vulnerable LGBTQ+ kids to their families. Because of family rejection, LGBTQ+ children (especially trans kids) are more likely to experience homelessness than other kids and are at higher risk of self-harm than other kids.
This cruel Initiative would strip kids’ privacy, causing family conflict, increased youth homelessness, and worsen the teen mental illness crisis. Vote “NO” on Initiative Measure No. IL26-001.

Mandatory sex inspections of young girls is not a phrase any of us wants to be writing, any of you want to be reading, or anyone should ever want to require. This initiative, bafflingly, claims to be about “defending equity in interscholastic sports” while prohibiting a tiny number of trans students from participating in sports and subjecting all girls to a mandatory inspection to confirm their biological sex.

Still need a reason to vote no? No Hate in Washington State calls I-638 “The most extreme MAGA measure of its kind in the U.S., I-638 would require tens of thousands of elementary, middle and high school girls (but not boys) to undergo intrusive, potentially harmful medical sex inspections every year as a new part of sports physicals.”

Call us old-fashioned, but we think youth sports are supposed to be about having fun, encouraging physical activity, teamwork, and leadership skills, not about unnecessary and invasive medical inspections or imposed gender conformity. We’re proud to join the Washington State PTA , the Washington Education Association , League of Women Voters , and many, many more in opposing this awful initiative. Vote no on I-638.

We’ve been screaming from the rooftops for years that if we want to get this state on track, we absolutely must fix our regressive, upside-down tax code. It’s also wildly popular and works like a charm . It’s why we support the capital gains tax and defended it when hedge fund manager Brian Heywood tried to repeal it in 2024. And it’s why the millionaires tax is another huge step forward in making meaningful change in our struggling state budget so that we can continue to have the way of life in Washington that people love.

Like the attempted capital gains tax repeal, this new attack on the millionaires tax would upend our budget if passed and defund our schools and healthcare. The ballot measure, listed as IP26-645, was forced onto the ballot by a multi-million-dollar signature-gathering campaign funded by Haywood and his rich friends, hoping to shrink their tax bills – even though the richest 1% already pay a lower tax rate than the vast majority of middle-class Washingtonians.

First, let’s get some facts straight. This tax is narrower than simply being a millionaire: the tax applies to income over a million dollars per year (less than 20,000 households) and would only apply after that millionth dollar. If you make $1,000,100 in one year, your tax burden would be $9.90.

Despite that narrow pool and large deduction, it’s projected to bring in over $3 billion per year to fund schools, child care, healthcare, and reduce/eliminate other taxes everyday people pay. In other words: with the millionaires tax, most people pay less in taxes, small businesses pay less in taxes, and the ultrawealthy pay a little bit more towards their fair share. Without it, we lose big on the things that matter most to us.

What would you do with a million extra bus hours? Well, the Seattle Transit Measure is investing them in more frequency, more weekend service, more midday service, and more late-night service. Plus, the transit measure would fund more free ORCA passes for low-income riders. This renewal would take all of the bonus investments that Seattle has infused into Metro service and amplify it, in addition to funding the streetcar system and more.

Everyone should be able to get to where they’re going at any time of day in a world-class city like Seattle. We deserve to be able to make it to the kids’ soccer games on weekends, make it home from a night out or a late shift, and have regular, frequent service throughout the day.

Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposal doubles the size of the transit measure, raising about $138 million annually by increasing the measure’s sales tax from 0.15% to 0.3%. That would give Seattle extra purchasing power, with 280,000 bus service hours to invest annually instead of the 180,000 previously. Seattle and Metro expect at least 10 of the city’s busiest buses to see augmented service over current levels.

Because this is a renewal of existing revenue, if the measure were to fail, we would lose funds, lose service hours, lose frequency, and lose big altogether. While sales taxes are regressive, cutting bus service is far more regressive.
Hop on board, Seattle. Vote Yes on Prop 1.

Just as critically, Pierce County absolutely must pass its own transit measure . It’s also a small sales tax increase, but it would similarly mean more buses, running to more places, more often. It also makes buses fare-free for seniors. So much good would come of the investments into Pierce Transit that this measure enables.
Prop 1 would increase service levels by more than 40%, a massive infusion for a county that has lagged behind on transit investment.

If approved, the ballot measure would bump the dedicated sales tax rate funding Pierce Transit from 0.6% to 0.9%, a funding stream that has been sitting unchanged since George W. Bush's first term in the White House. That would put Pierce County in closer parity with neighboring counties, which boast more frequent bus service.

With the added funding, Pierce Transit expects to be able to add four brand new routes across Tacoma and Puyallup, extend hours on 23 routes, and boost frequencies on 21 routes to run at least every 20 to 30 minutes on the weekends, compared to just four routes clearing that basic bar for frequency today.

When we think about how people get around, where they get around and how we can connect communities across the sound, Pierce has to be a part of that picture. It’s not just about Tacoma. Whether you live in Puyallup or Gig Harbor, Steilacoom or Fife, you deserve transit access and reliable service.

While Seattle often passes transit funding measures by comfortable margins, the same is not true of Pierce County, which saw its last transit measures fail in 2011 and 2012. It’s going to be a tight race to get it passed, so it’s important to vote yes and talk to your neighbors about how important it is that they do, too!

Tenant protections only matter if they’re enforced. Tacoma passed the 2023 Tenant Bill of Rights, but supporters say tenants face retaliation or struggle to afford the private legal actions required for accountability. The Tacoma For All Coalition, which backed the measure, said “just one fine against a law-breaking landlord has been issued” since the 2023 law went into effect.

Tacoma’s Measure 1 (Safe Homes For All) seeks to protect tenant unions and ratchet up fines on noncompliant landlords. The measure isn’t perfect – enforcement will be funded in a small, per-unit rental fee, but repeat offenders will also pay into enforcement costs, a strategic compromise to ensure it does not come at the expense of other essential city services.

articles.title: Five years of katsu on 15th Ave E: Kobuta & Ookami looks back, and north to Mountlake Terrace
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: When Kobuta & Ookami finally opened its doors on 15th Ave E in fall 2021, Sue Phuksopha wasn’t sure anybody would show up. The partners had signed their lease before COVID-19 shut everything down, then watched construction stall for months. When opening day came, they found a line waiting outside.
“After waiting so long and not knowing what was going to happen, seeing that line made us so happy and excited,” Phuksopha told CHS.

Five years later, the katsu specialist has grown into a small family of restaurants , Capitol Hill and Redmond today, with a third location planned for Mountlake Terrace in 2027. CHS caught up with the team to talk about what’s changed, what hasn’t, and why Seattle can’t seem to get enough fried pork cutlet.
The pandemic delay turned out to have a silver lining. Because rent didn’t kick in until the space was turned over, the partners used the extra months to refine recipes and the menu.

Opening was still a challenge. Kobuta & Ookami debuted as dine-in only at a time when people were still uneasy about sitting down inside a restaurant. Staff checked vaccination cards and worked to make both customers and employees feel safe.
“We thought we would have a little more time to adjust, but we had to learn very quickly,” Phuksopha said. “All of us as partners learned different positions and jumped in wherever we were needed.”
When the restaurant opened, Phuksopha told CHS they wanted to capture the casual street-dining vibe of the little alleys in Japan. That’s still the goal.

“When we travel there, we really love the little restaurants, the alleys, places under the train tracks, just sitting down with good food, sake, beer or a highball, spending time with friends and enjoying yourself,” Phuksopha said.

The team still travels to Japan at least once a year. “We like to call it ‘research,’ but really, we just love going there,” Phuksopha said, and they always come back with new ideas for food, drinks and atmosphere.

When it first opened, CHS marked Kobuta & Ookami as a first for the neighborhood. After years of mixed-use development bringing new buildings with brand new restaurant spaces to Capitol Hill, 2021 marked the beginning of the development slowdown. Kobuta & Ookami’s September debut was the first and one of the only food and drink debuts in a fresh restaurant space part of a new development that year.

The restaurant has become more than expected, with longtime regulars, families, visitors brought in by out-of-town friends, and customers who have followed them from Capitol Hill to Redmond. Phuksopha credits much of that growth to word of mouth, along with coverage from local media including CHS.
Despite five years of tinkering, the menu’s heart hasn’t moved. “Katsu is always going to be the heart of Kobuta & Ookami,” Phuksopha said.

A few appetizers and entrées have been added along the way, but the team has kept things deliberately tight. A smaller menu means faster service and more consistent training, essential in the tiny Capitol Hill dining room and kitchen. Many of the dishes from the original menu remain among the most popular today.
The biggest surprise of running a katsu-focused restaurant? “Probably how much people really love katsu!”

The dish looks simple, Phuksopha said, but the pork, breading, oil, temperature, texture and timing all matter, and customers notice. Keeping something that simple consistent every day takes constant work on staffing, training and equipment.
“Five years later, we’re still learning.”
As for why customers keep coming back, Phuksopha points to comfort, consistency and price. “It’s crispy, hot, satisfying and simple. When it’s done well, you crave it,” they said.
Phuksopha wants Kobuta & Ookami to be an everyday spot rather than a special-occasion splurge, something that has gotten harder with inflation, tariffs and rising ingredient costs.
The neighborhood around the restaurant has shifted, too. Phuksopha and crew have watched businesses open and close and new residents move in.
Kobuta & Ookami is part of a cluster of Capitol Hill food and drink in this block of 15th Ave E with Bakery Nouveau, Teriyaki Madness , and Aviv Hummus Bar nearby.

Lunch has gotten quieter as work patterns have changed, pushing the team to think more creatively about giving people reasons to stop by on weekdays. They also cited more visible homelessness and concerns about safety and property crime in their of Capitol Hill, saying they hope those issues continue to get attention so staff, customers and neighbors feel safe.

Then there are costs. Food, labor, insurance, utilities, “Inflation has affected almost everything,” they said. “Restaurants already operate on pretty small margins, so trying to keep prices reasonable while maintaining quality and taking care of our staff gets harder every year.”
There’s more competition, too, but Phuksopha say they’d rather focus on their own food and service.
“Capitol Hill is where Kobuta & Ookami started, so that location will always be really special to us.”
The team came to katsu from a Thai food background, but their love of Japanese food, animation and culture goes back to childhood. Travel deepened that appreciation, and changed how they eat.
“Before, we were mostly just eating and thinking, ‘This is so good.’ Now our restaurant brains never completely turn off,” they said. Breading, oil, plates, signs, lighting, they notice all of it.

Sake and Sapporo can be an important part of the experience, and Phuksopha said they want to lean into the drinks side even more. The sake list rotates as the team tastes new bottles, with an emphasis on keeping things approachable.
“You shouldn’t have to know everything about sake to order a glass and enjoy it,” they said. “Obviously we can’t bring Japan to Seattle, but we can bring a little bit of that feeling here.”

The third Kobuta & Ookami is planned for Mountlake Terrace in 2027. Phuksopha said they chose the location partly because customers farther north kept telling them they wanted to visit without fighting traffic into Seattle or Redmond.

The bigger space will let the team lean further into the Japanese yokocho, or alley, feel, with more sake, Japanese-style drinks and highballs, and a few new dishes, while keeping tonkatsu at the center.
Over the next five years, Phuksopha wants each location to have its own personality while still feeling like Kobuta & Ookami. And down the line, maybe something entirely new.
“We have a lot of ideas, but nothing we’re ready to announce yet.”
Kobuta & Ookami is located at121 15th Ave E. Learn more at kobutaandookami.com .

articles.title: Seattle budget proposal would hike parking tax for commercial lots to 17%
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Drivers will pay steeper fees to leave cars in private lots and garages under a budget proposal to raise the city’s Commercial Parking Tax to help close City Hall’s budget shortfall.

The proposal would lift the tax from 14.5% to 17% in 2027, generating an extra $9.3 million annually. Because commercial parking is also subject to state and local retail sales taxes, the change pushes the total tax on paid stalls to 27.55%, adding roughly $5.50 in total taxes to a $20 parking charge.

The proposal is part of Mayor Katie Wilson’s plan to wipe out a $175 million deficit without tax increases or withdrawals from city reserves and now on the table as the Seattle City Council works to approve the city’s 2027-2028 budget over the coming weeks.

With the city confronting a general fund deficit, adopting the commercial parking tax increase allows lawmakers to shore up essential street maintenance and safety programs without diverting scarce general funds, leaning on parking revenue to patch the city’s balance sheet even as downtown businesses warn of the added cost on visitors.

Under the current 14.5% rate, Seattle collects approximately $50 million to $54 million per year from the Commercial Parking Tax from an estimated 400 to 600 commercial parking facilities with taxpayers concentrated among a much smaller group of management entities.

articles.title: Five Films To See at the Seattle Trans Underground Film Festival
articles.author: Chase Hutchinson
paras: The Seattle Trans Underground Film Festival (STUFF) returns this week, proving that independent and trans cinema is not only alive, but thriving. With a variety of features and shorts, it’s the local film festival to attend this week.
The fest runs October 15th through the 18th at the Northwest Film Forum ( now open all week long! ). Here are five highlights you definitely don’t want to miss.

Directed by May Matchim, the opening night feature is a queer ecology documentary about the diversity of sexuality and gender in what Matchim calls “the fantastically queer” place that is nature. Both self-reflexive and sincere, Amphibian is a film that doesn’t fall into easy boxes. It flags early on that it’s not going to use the framing of certain things being “natural” to make queerness more palatable. Instead, Amphibian evolves in scope and ambition, gently confronting some of its own preconceived notions and narratives to create a portrait of all the complex, layered beauty to be found in existence. Though largely relying on a variety of talking head interviews, Amphibian also taps into something personal as we hear Matchim reflect on her own journey to accepting her transness, culminating in a poignant reflection that ties it all together perfectly.
Showing Thursday, October 15 at 6:30 p.m.

Next is a film that bravely asks what if you took Bertrand Bonello’s Nocturama, shot it like a mockumentary, kept the terrorism, added some satanism, and centered two of the most chaotic (complimentary) people you’ll ever meet? Gren Bee’s Trans Panic! follows Christian trans hyperpop musician Sara ‘T-Girl Nixon’ Jordan (Mia Sabine) who links up with the insecure intersex incel filmmaker Cody ‘Yung AJ’ Jones (Gren Bee) in order to carry out a terrorist attack to launch a music career and possibly also catch the attention of JD Vance like a reverse John Hinckley Jr. What could possibly go wrong? As it turns out, quite a lot. The pseudo-hangout movie is off-kilter even before it descends into complete chaos. But for those who can get on its wavelength, Trans Panic! ‘s cheeky provocations and freewheeling approach pay off and build to a bloody finale that gets its pound of flesh and then some.

Raef Van Putten’s Jucks is an experimental sci-fi silent film with the most striking visuals of the festival. Shot entirely in black-and-white, it takes us far into the future—2064 AD, to be precise—with a troubled protagonist known as Jules as they navigate a dystopian hellscape (Denver City) in search of gold. This description still only barely scratches the surface of what’s in store for you as this film. Without any spoken words, it boasts an entrancing, droning score that doubles as an all-consuming radio frequency in the film, drowning everything else out. For those who can surrender themselves to this oddity, they’ll find something truly spellbinding.
Showing Saturday, October 17 at 4:30 p.m.

Louise Weard’s Castration Movie Chapter iii.ii Junior Ghosts—Premorphic Drift; a fragmentary passage is the feel-bad movie of the festival. For those not familiar with Weard’s filmography, this is one of several Castration Movies and lifts its characters from a prior entry. However, no prior Castration knowledge is required, as this one tells a self-contained story. And it’s Weard’s best entry yet. Following Izzy (played by Avalon Fast) as she desperately tries to stop her partner, Tiffany (Henri Gillespi), from transitioning, the film is both funnier and more painful than it sounds. Weard brings plenty of satirical bite to key scenes before bringing down the emotional hammer in the intimate moments between the couple. While you’ll feel a pit in your stomach all the way until the final lines, you’ll be hard-pressed to find a more potent character study at the festival this year.

Last but definitely not least is Deathbed (no, not 1977’s Death Bed: The Bed That Eats ). Rather, this film is a scrappy, bite-sized, lo-fi local gem, about a haunting that disrupts a friend group. It’s filmed across Seattle (including in the Northwest Film Forum itself!). This already makes it worth seeing for that alone, but it’s also got some other tricks up its sleeves. Without giving anything away, there are some sinister scenes where the picture begins to distort and warp, drawing you in before snapping back to “normal.” Even when it’s a little rough around the edges, this is a feature, not a bug, with the crackling and distorting audio getting under your skin. It builds to visuals of ghosts taking shape out of static that may just haunt you as well.
Showing Sunday, October 18 at 7:30 p.m. as part of the WE LIVE shorts program

articles.title: Slog AM: Woman Raped at UW Fraternity Sues University, Right-Wing Radio Unhappy About Yakima Judge’s Advice for Avoiding ICE, Trump Posts AI Video of Himself Playing With Tiger that Killed UK Man
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: Yesterday, it was reported that Cornell University suspended frat parties in response to the public’s outrage at its exposed attempt to sweep gang rape allegations under the rug. Today, KIRO reports that “a woman who was raped at a University of Washington fraternity house in 2022” is not only suing the university but also the man convicted of the rape. She alleges that UW knew that the rapist had a record in the form of a “restraining order involving alleged sexual misconduct” but failed to do anything meaningful about it, and so ultimately failed to protect her. What will not surprise anyone, is another report of this kind being filed tomorrow and the day after that.

Seattle’s top right-wing radio personality , Jason Rantz, is upset because Yakima Municipal Court Presiding Judge Aryn Masters “has found a way to help criminal defendants dodge federal immigration agents”: Just skip court; don’t show up; stay the hell away. Why? Because ICE does not play by the rules. Indeed, it is the grimy business of these hoodlums to break laws and needlessly cause, what Fela Kuti called, when describing the thugs the Nigerian government of his times employed: “Sorrow Tears and Blood.” That’s their “regular trademark.”

Now, how can a court do its work when ICE makes arrests at a justice center “without clearing it with the court first?” Where is the law and order in that? And what’s with the fucking masks? The unmarked cars?? The near lack of non-lethal equipment and training??? In the case of the Yakima Municipal Court, the law must protect itself from those that do not recognize and operate within the limits of the law. Even the defendant who shows up for a hearing is doing something ICE refuses to do: follow the law.

Sunworshipers, enjoy today and the rest of the week because starting this weekend warmth will bid farewell to you all and turn over the keys of the seasons to autumn. The Wednesday that appeared when you left the confounding region of dreams or the grinding region of insomnia will have some clouds, some wind, maybe a little light rain, and even clear skies here and there. Expect a high of 66.

I have nothing to say about Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia . Watch her first encounter with the press yesterday and you will see why nothing has to be said. Nothing can only be reflected by nothing, like a vampire looking into a mirror. But I much prefer those nocturnal and aristocratic bloodsuckers to this standard issued from the void of Trump’s political nothingness. Please vote in November.

Speaking of mirrors , according to a recent story filed by Abdul Moeed, “Ancient Greek and Roman Beliefs About the Evil Eye Reflected in Miniature Mirror,” back in the dusty pagan days near the beginning of the previous millennium, little mirrors were used to protect the living and the dead from the “evil eye.” These supernatural mirrors were worn, hung from candles, placed next to the bed or in graves to check bad luck and other misfortunes. Researchers Eli Buchman and Adi Erlich published their study of the pagan mirrors in Palestine Exploration Quarterly .

One more on mirrors. This is a passage in Stanisław Lem’s mid-century science fiction novel Solaris : “We head out into space, ready for anything, which is to say, for solitude, arduous work, self-sacrifice, and death. Out of modesty we don’t say it aloud, but from time to time we think about how magnificent we are… That’s another falsity. We’re not searching for anything except people. We don’t need other worlds. We need mirrors.”

Remember the young man who , on October 10, jumped into an enclosure at the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, which is on the outskirts of Doncaster, UK. Recall, if you saw the gruesome video, how he got mauled to death by a massive and very pissed tiger. Well, last night President Trump posted on Truth Social an AI video of himself in the Yorkshire enclosure confronting, then defeating, then becoming besties with the tiger that killed the 23-year-old Brit. Yes, there is lots of outrage about all of this. But, to be honest, I hope Trump sticks to posting this dumb, insensitive, crassly unfunny AI garbage and leaves the real world ( Ilhan Omar , Oscar Belgal , and so on) alone.

As for Katie Miller , the wife of one of the most sadistic members of Trump’s administration, Stephen Miller, thank you for posting this on X right after thugs raided Ilhan Omar’s Washington, DC, home on Monday: “Promise made, promise kept.” The post was soon deleted, but not soon enough. Mere seconds (if not the very second) it entered cyberspace, it entered all of eternity. And if voters like myself “live through this,” as the title of Hole album puts it, we will surely be pleased to see the ghost of that post revived in court.

The 42-year-old man, Hassan Kariem , who, on Monday, died after being ejected from a Six Flags Over Georgia roller coaster called Goliath, had, according to his daughter , in the past defeated cancer (which is no joke when you’re young), won “a tough battle with COVID-19,” and “survived a car fire.” But the chances of Kariem beating a mean and faulty theme park machine with a 200-foot drop and a top speed of 70 mph was close to, if not exactly, zero.

Let’s end AM with a late-70s afrobeat (not to be confused with contemporary afrobeats ) that accurately describes the sole function of the Trump/Miller Gang called ICE, Fela Kuti’s “Sorrow Tears and Blood.”

articles.title: Yemen’s Houthis are bringing their war to Saudi Arabia – and reframing the narrative of being an Iranian proxy
articles.author:
<name>Laurent Bonnefoy, CNRS research fellow, Center for International Studies, Sciences Po</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/laurent-bonnefoy-2771004"/>
paras: A deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh’s international airport has highlighted how the Yemeni group is reframing its perceived “Iran proxy” role and shifting its regional focus to its ongoing battle against Saudi Arabia. The Oct. 10 strike, in which 13 people were killed and hundreds injured, was the most violent episode on Saudi Arabian soil since the beginning of the war in Iran in February.
It was followed by further – albeit less deadly – missile barrages in the days since. The violence, moreover, comes just as the kingdom is hosting a major conference for oil producers.

As a longtime analyst of Yemeni politics , I see the latest attacks as another illustration of both the expanding regional stalemate across the Middle East and the need to understand how Yemen’s decade-long war is having effects far beyond its territory.

The Houthi movement first emerged as a militarized political actor in Yemen in 2004 and has been locked in a multiyear civil war against the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed central government. Currently, the Houthis control about a third of the territory and two-thirds of the population. They are undoubtedly Yemen’s most powerful armed force, despite lacking access to warplanes, and have developed an arsenal of long-range missiles and drones.
All along, the Houthis have frequently been portrayed by their adversaries and many external observers as a proxy for Iran, the chief regional rival to Saudi Arabia.

It’s true that the movement has long been broadly aligned with Tehran and frequently shared regional objections, even if the relationship is complex and varied . At the same time, the evolution of the Houthi movement remains intimately connected to Yemen’s domestic political context and to a historical feud specific to the country – something I and many other scholars have researched.

What is particularly significant in the current context of an escalating fight with Saudi Arabia, however, is the way in which the Houthi leadership has sought to reframe its military engagement over the course of 2026 so that it does not appear to be directed by Iran.
This shift is analytically important because it reveals how Houthi leaders understand the political effectiveness of particular narratives and how they seek to legitimize their actions.

When the United States and Israel launched their attack on Iran on Feb. 28, many observers expected the Houthis to enter the conflict swiftly. Their previous intervention in the Red Sea – between November 2023 and May 2025 – in support of Palestinians after Israel’s war in Gaza had, to some extent, provided a blueprint for disrupting maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

The symbolic returns of their earlier campaign had been considerable. On the one hand, it demonstrated the Houthis’ willingness to act in support of Gaza at a time when many Arab governments were widely perceived as turning their backs on the plight of Palestinians. It also revealed the movement’s capacity to disrupt global supply chains and affect international trade far beyond Yemen.

But the Houthis remained on the sidelines for several months after the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Their leaders appeared to disregard reports that Iranian decision-makers had called on them , in July 2026, to close the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb to maritime traffic.

Assuming that the Houthis would automatically act at Tehran’s command reflected a misreading of Yemeni history and of the identity markers that shape the movement’s political legitimacy. Acting in support of Palestinians could be framed for a domestic and regional audience as an expression of Arab solidarity. But acting on behalf of Iran, a non-Arab Persian country composed almost entirely of Twelver Shia Muslims , was considerably more difficult to rationalize in Arab Yemen where Twelver Shia Muslims are absent and Sunnis are the majority.
The Houthis’ reentry into the regional conflict in August took place alongside a shift in their political narrative, which increasingly centered on their long-standing adversary, Saudi Arabia.

Although the strategic consequences of their actions may ultimately benefit Iran in its own regional and international conflicts, the Houthis see their military campaign against Saudi Arabia chiefly as an act of national defense.

During the summer of 2026, an important episode went largely unnoticed in the Western media: the Houthis’ attempt to establish the reopening of Sanaa International Airport through the surprise departure of a Tehran-bound flight and its subsequent return.

The airport, located in the Houthi-controlled capital, had been closed since late 2024 following Israeli strikes . Its continued closure meant that access to and exit from Houthi-controlled territory remained subject to restrictions imposed by the movement’s adversaries. These included the authorities controlling Aden, the interim capital of the internationally recognized government.

From the Houthis’ perspective, their sovereignty consequently remained incomplete. The airport’s closure not only restricted civilian movement but also limited their ability to send supporters abroad for training and potentially to receive military equipment. On July 13, the Saudi military’s subsequent bombing of the Sanaa runway, as the incoming aircraft from Tehran approached, provided the movement an opportunity to reignite its confrontation with Riyadh.

After more than three years of a de facto ceasefire and difficult negotiations, Riyadh appeared, as in its dealings with Iran, increasingly eager to extricate itself from the region’s protracted conflicts. Sensing an opening, the Houthi leadership responded by invoking a logic of tit-for-tat retaliation.

The Houthis’ tactics today are a kind of mirror to the 2015 launch of a Saudi-led bombing campaign and blockade of the Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen that has led to years of protracted civil war. The Houthis now claim the right to impose reciprocal restrictions on Saudi Arabia, particularly by targeting its ports and oil-exporting infrastructure.

The Houthis’ new tactic serves two purposes. First, it allows the Houthis to redirect responsibility for the economic and humanitarian crisis in and around Sanaa toward the Saudi-enforced blockade rather than their own governance failures, mismanagement and corruption. Second, it provides a rationale for escalating the conflict across the region.

Previously, the Houthi military leadership had halted attacks on Israeli-linked shipping in the Red Sea following the formal Gaza ceasefire of October 2025, despite having repeatedly come under bombardment. It had likewise suspended attacks on American vessels following an agreement with the Trump administration in May 2025.

These decisions demonstrated a degree of pragmatism beneath the movement’s inflammatory rhetoric. That pragmatism appeared to persist even as the Houthis resumed their regional military engagement, with American diplomats reportedly meeting Houthi representatives in Oman in September 2026.

With Saudi Arabia, however, the Houthis felt less compunction. Riyadh was already facing repeated barrages of Iran missiles as a consequences of its alliance with the U.S. and facing an energy export squeeze. So with the Saudi airport incident, the Houthi leadership feels it has trapped Saudi Arabia , with consequences extending to the global economy.

This retaliatory strategy was bolstered by successful Houthi moves in early September to establish a degree of control over the Strait of Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important maritime choke points. That gave the Houthis leverage over shipping crucial for Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea.
Drones and ballistic missiles, as the attacks on the Riyadh airport illustrate, also give the movement the capacity to strike targets across much of Saudi Arabia.
The targeting of civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, particularly airports, illustrates the retaliatory logic the Houthis have invoked to justify their actions.

It’s far from clear what the consequences of this increasingly aggressive Houthi campaign will be. The region seems poised for ongoing strife, and it’s an open question whether it will draw back in the likes of the U.S., which has been reluctant to return to full-scale regional conflict.

Yet none of that should obscure the plight of civilians in Yemen. Rather, it should serve as a reminder of the suffering of a population exhausted by a war that has lasted for more than a decade and has devastated the already meager infrastructure of what was the poorest country in the Middle East even before the conflict started.

articles.title: Philly voters care about local issues, but election integrity fears make them wonder if their vote matters
articles.author:
<name>Heather LaMarre, Associate Professor of Media and Communication, Temple University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/heather-lamarre-174445"/>
paras: Less than 30 days ahead of the 2026 midterms and almost nobody I talk to in Philadelphia is excited. Not my neighbors. Not my students or colleagues at Temple University, where I research and teach political communication and public opinion . Not even my politically engaged friends.
This mirrors the national mood in recent years: In a Pew Research Center survey , just 4% of Americans said they feel excited about politics; 65% said they feel exhausted.

“There are many factors that go into voter apathy,” explains Temple University political communications professor Bruce Hardy, “barriers to participation, lack of trust, cynicism, sense of disenfranchisement and powerlessness, political fatigue, and so on.”
Voter malaise and campaign fatigue aren’t new, but something feels different to me this time.

Lauren Cristella, president and CEO of the Committee of Seventy , a nonpartisan organization established to improve the voting process and engage Philadelphia citizens in the democratic process, agrees. She points to election integrity fears being hotly debated in the national media as part of the problem.

“We are sitting on the back side of a big decline in voter enthusiasm ,” she said, “And yes, we need to start giving voters something to be excited about. However, what we are seeing in the commonwealth is a lot of confusion and fear around election integrity.”
This tension, in my view, is the real story of the 2026 midterms. Voters still care. The stakes are higher than ever. But the question on many voters’ minds is: Will my vote even count?

This is not just a Philadelphia problem. A July 2026 Gallup survey of more than 23,000 adults found that 2 in 3 Americans were concerned about political leaders pressuring election officials to change outcomes. Half worried that their own ballot would not be counted.

Voter confidence is sliding. In a 2026 University of California San Diego survey , 49% of Americans said they expect the midterms to be free and fair, while 51% expect unfair elections or aren’t sure.

A 2026 Pew survey similarly found that barely half of Americans are confident that November’s midterm elections will be conducted fairly and accurately. This represents a 10-point drop in national voter confidence from 61% in the 2024 elections.

Social and behavioral scientists have long understood the tension between one’s beliefs and attitudes about voting: For example, many people say they believe voting is an important democratic behavior, but then don’t actually vote themselves.

Efforts to close the gap between people’s intentions to vote and getting them to actually vote are where issues like mail-in voting , polling locations , time off work and voter ID laws make a difference.

Voting by mail has been a flash point since the 2020 presidential election when Philadelphia and Pennsylvania sat at the center of controversy . However, this should not be an issue for Philadelphians – or Pennsylvanians – in the upcoming midterms. The U.S. Supreme Court recently blocked a federal attempt to impose new Postal Service rules limiting mail-in voting.
Cristella told me that mail-in voting is “the safest and most secure of any time in the commonwealth’s history.” Every ballot can be tracked .
So why are Pennsylvania voters not convinced?

A 2021 article that cites experts at Tufts University explains how pushing myths like the “election was stolen” or “the election wasn’t fair” – presumably to explain away Donald Trump’s loss in 2020 and create mobilization for his 2024 presidential run – can boomerang and end up lowering confidence in future elections.

If people don’t believe their vote will count, then it becomes completely rational to simultaneously hold the opinion that voting is generally good for democracy, while also lacking any faith that their own vote will even be counted.
Framing theory explains how the presentation of information in the media influences the way people process and interpret it.

Hardy attributes much of the current state of voter apathy to the media’s focus on fraud and voter integrity. He says that “much of this comes from political discourse and media focusing on national political conflict, a seemingly endless election cycle, and a constant reinforcement of political in-groups and out-groups.”

Even though our elections are safe and secure in Philadelphia, he explains, “All of this negative national media coverage can overshadow the importance of local elections and leave people feeling disengaged from the politics closest to home.”
Cristella agrees that media framing is a significant part of the problem.

“Issues surrounding election fraud and vote integrity get amplified and muddied,” she said. When isolated issues in other states occur, even if proved untrue, the intense and repeated national media attention on them shakes voter confidence here at home.

The 2026 midterms will be an important election for Pennsylvania, as the election will determine the state’s next governor and lieutenant governor, as well as members of the U.S. House of Representatives and the state Legislature.

Economic concerns, in particular, are a major issue this election. A recent Gallup poll indicates that confidence in the economy is at its weakest level since 2022. And the voters are feeling the pinch.
While the 2026 Philadelphia primary had a low 22% turnout , Cristella believes issues like affordability will lead to a strong turnout in November.
As a longtime Philadelphian who believes strongly in our democracy, I am staying hopeful.
Pennsylvania has 40,000 poll workers for each election. To become a poll worker, visit vote.phila.gov or vote.pa.gov .
Read more of our stories about Philadelphia and Pennsylvania , or sign up for our Philadelphia newsletter on Substack .

articles.title: Republicans can confirm a Supreme Court justice if Democrats take the Senate, but at what cost?
articles.author:
<name>Paul M. Collins Jr., Professor of Legal Studies and Political Science, UMass Amherst</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/paul-m-collins-jr-241509"/>
paras: Democrats are gaining momentum in their bid to retake the Senate in November . This has led Republicans to prepare for the possibility that a conservative Supreme Court justice might announce their retirement before the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027 .
This would give President Donald Trump his fourth Supreme Court nomination, helping to ensure conservative dominance on the court for decades.

As a Supreme Court scholar , I know that judicial appointments have real consequences. Look no further than Roe v. Wade : Within two years of securing a 6–3 conservative majority, the high court in 2022 eliminated the constitutional right to abortion that had existed for almost 50 years.
If Democrats take over the Senate and a Republican-appointed justice retires before Jan. 3, this will trigger one of the most explosive confirmation battles in American history.
Here’s how the fight is likely to play out – and why the stakes are so high.

Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas top the list of potential retirees should Democrats win the Senate in November. Alito and Thomas are the court’s oldest justices, at 76 and 78, respectively. Thomas is also the court’s longest-serving justice, appointed by President George H.W. Bush in 1991.

Perhaps more importantly, both justices have deep ties to the conservative legal movement . This is a network of lawyers, judges and politicians who seek to etch conservative principles into law. Overturning Roe v. Wade was at the top of the conservative wish list .
My research suggests that both Alito and Thomas care about their legacies . And they both understand that a Democratic-controlled Senate would block another Trump-appointed nominee.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer made this clear on Oct. 5, 2026, as did Senate Judiciary Committee member Richard Blumenthal, the Democrat from Connecticut. Blumenthal said , “It is slim to none that we would support a nominee from this administration.”

Though Alito has recently indicated he intends to stay on the court through its 2026 term, Thomas has made no recent public statements about retirement. And Alito is free to change his mind at any time.

If Alito or Thomas announced their retirement after the midterms, Republicans would have enough time to confirm a successor. The Senate has four and a half work weeks scheduled between Election Day and Jan. 3. Justice Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed less than a month after her nomination, making the timeline tight but doable.

Democrats will likely attempt to slow down the process, but they face an uphill battle with few options. Republicans stripped away key delaying tactics in recent years by ending the filibuster in 2017 and ignoring the Judiciary Committee’s quorum rules in 2020. This rule requires nine members be present to transact business, including two members of the minority party.
A Republican effort to confirm a Supreme Court nominee during a lame-duck Senate would spark a historic battle with Democrats.

Democrats would surely point to how Republicans handled President Barack Obama’s appointment of Merrick Garland in 2016. A seat on the court opened up after conservative Antonin Scalia died on Feb. 13, almost nine months before the November presidential election.

Republicans refused to move Garland’s nomination through the confirmation process, using their majority power to set the Senate’s agenda . This marked the first time since 1866 that a Supreme Court nomination that was not withdrawn failed to receive an up-or-down vote in the Senate.

To justify this, Republicans created the so-called “ McConnell Rule ,” named after former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky. According to McConnell , the Senate should not fill Supreme Court vacancies “in the middle of a presidential election year.”
Four years later, Senate Republicans abruptly abandoned the rule . This allowed them to push through Coney Barrett’s confirmation just days before the 2020 presidential election.
Democrats did not take kindly to this reversal.
Schumer pulled no punches in a speech the day of Barrett’s confirmation vote. Schumer said the day “will go down as one of the darkest days in the 231-year history of the United States Senate.”

He alleged the Republican majority made “a mockery of its own stated principle – that the American people deserve a voice in the selection of Supreme Court Justices – completing the partisan theft of two seats on the Supreme Court using completely contradictory rationales.”
Democrats were clearly outraged by what they saw as two stolen Supreme Court seats.
However, I believe that pushing through a nominee will trigger an even fiercer fight. Senate Democrats will see such a confirmation as a power grab that sidelines the voice of voters.
Furthermore, if a Republican justice retires should Democrats win the Senate, the move will almost certainly be viewed as purely partisan.

This has the potential to further erode public support for the court , which is sitting near historic lows . And it will likely fuel the fire of Supreme Court reform, including the possibility of expanding the number of justices on the court .
Put simply, in securing a short-term conservative victory, Republicans may end up handing Democrats the exact justification they need to reshape the high court.
