articles.title: Relaunched Community Court Gets Paired With Punitive Repeat Offender System
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: The Seattle City Attorney’s Office (CAO) has announced two new programs affecting its handling of misdemeanor criminal cases in Seattle: a new community court called Connections Court and a new repeat offender system called the High-Priority Repeat Offenses (HiPRO) program. Both programs are being launched despite concerns expressed by the King County Department of Public Defense (DPD).

“Connection Court restores a key prosecution alternative with new accountability, and our HiPRO protocols seek firmer consequences for those who have taken advantage of Seattle's compassion,” Seattle City Attorney Erika Evans said in a press release.

Evans took office at the beginning of the year after delivering a rousing defeat to the former City Attorney, Republican Ann Davison. On the campaign trail, Evans promised to undo many of the harms of her predecessor, including beginning a new community court program to replace the one Davison had unilaterally shut down.
Less than ten months after taking office, Evans is delivering on that promise.

“Connection Court is a much-welcomed successor to its failed predecessors for importantly it centers on the participants and their needs but also accountability,” said Seattle Councilmember Bob Kettle, the chair of the public safety committee . “ I thank City Attorney Evans for furthering a more functional criminal justice system, which is crucial in creating a safer Seattle.”

Not everyone is as happy about Evans’ changes to this iteration of community court, the previous version of which was launched in 2020 by former City Attorney Pete Holmes. The biggest critic of the new programs is King County DPD.

Being the watchdog of CAO is nothing new for DPD, which spoke out against many of Davison’s policies. In addition to objecting to Davison’s ending of the former community court program, DPD opposed Davison’s High Utilizers Initiative and her Stay Out of Drug Area (SODA) and Stay Out of Areas of Prostitution (SOAP) exclusion orders . The department also drew attention to Davison’s enforcement of Seattle’s 2023 drug ordinance, which had a disproportionate impact on Black people based on City data and wasn’t resulting in the promised diversion.

Some hoped that with Evans in office, there would be a new ability of CAO and DPD to cooperate. But DPD told The Urbanist that Evans’ office didn’t inform them about the new HiPRO program until Monday, October 5, the day the new community court opened. As of Thursday afternoon, DPD hadn’t received any written protocols on the new system.

“I would say that we are disappointed by the HiPRO initiative and by the restrictions on who's eligible for Connection Court,” DPD’s Special Counsel for Criminal Policy and Practice Katie Hurley told The Urbanist .

On the criminal side, CAO only handles lower-level cases – misdemeanors and gross misdemeanors – while felonies are handled by the King County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office (KCPAO). In practice, this distinction means that many of the referrals CAO receives from the Seattle Police Department (SPD) involve crimes of poverty, oftentimes with a nexus of behavioral health conditions, although the office also handles some domestic violence and driving-under-the-influence cases.
Going forward, people who have been charged with a low-level, nonviolent offense without a pattern of repeated criminal misconduct may be sent through Evans’ new Connection Court.

“How I sum up Connection Court, it’s an opportunity to provide meaningful services to participants in the program so they get what they need to be okay, and then after 90 days, their case gets dismissed,” Evans told The Urbanist . “That is the summary of it, and I want it also really clear that we are still very robust in pre-file and post-file diversion, and this is just an additional layer.”

The new court program is being run at no additional cost to the City, providing an assessment with a court counselor to participants to determine which services would be the most appropriate for their individual needs. Evans talked about a menu of different services that includes medication-assisted substance use disorder treatment, help applying for health insurance, prescription delivery, mental health treatment, food, and ORCA cards. Participants will also have the opportunity to apply for jobs as downtown ambassadors with the Metropolitan Improvement District.

Evans is hoping to expand the program in the future, potentially hosting it at a local library and providing pet fostering for people who want to go into substance use treatment. And she has been in conversation with the Mayor’s Office about the possibility of setting aside a certain number of tiny homes or other shelter spots for participants in the program.

“I am very optimistic and hopeful that as we continue to grow and what we're able to provide for Connection Court, that the opportunity to have beds set aside for folks going through Connection Court is not only possible, but an absolute need for folks that are participating in the program,” Evans said.
Connection Court has a few key differences from its predecessor. These differences, which Kettle applauded, are points of contention between Evans’ office and DPD.

In the past, participants in community court would have their cases dismissed upon completion of the program, a policy supported by DPD. However, Evans has insisted on a 90-day jurisdiction period, regardless of how long the program engagements take, during which participants will need to avoid arrest in order to successfully complete the program. Participants also have to prove they’ve engaged with at least two different services.
Failure to meet either of these requirements and they could be sent back to mainstream court for criminal prosecution.

“We have to have a longer period to make sure we're actually engaging with participants,” Evans said. “I want to make sure that this is something that's going to be successful, and I know from us doing these cases, that's not in one day.”
DPD, on the other hand, believes cases should be dismissed when a participant successfully completes their engagement.

DPD also opposes stricter eligibility rules to the program. Evans has instituted eligibility restrictions for Connections Court based on prior criminal history, another change from the former community court. And Hurley said people will also be excluded if they are being held in custody for another offense, possibly because they are unable to afford their bail.

“We're really alarmed at that exclusion as well, as it denies the Connection Court pathway for people because they're not able to afford bail, and that's related to a case, a charge, where they're presumed innocent,” Hurley said.
Finally, people who are routed to the new HiPRO initiative won’t be eligible for Connection Court.

“These restrictions exclude the very people for whom a Connection Court is really most needed: those people struggling with homelessness, with behavioral health, who need support and help addressing underlying issues, rather than an aggravated jail sentence,” Hurley said.

The new HiPRO program will apply to cases where people who have been charged by the CAO either three times in three months or six times in six months. In addition, cases can be routed into the program immediately if a person has shoplifted in a store where they have previously been trespassed or if they’re being charged for a car prowl case (breaking into a vehicle) and have a conviction of felony theft, car theft, or robbery in the last year.
People with a case flagged for the HiPRO program will be ineligible for either diversion or Connection Court, and attorneys will ask for longer sentences for these cases.

“We're making sure we're giving folks opportunities for those services and treatment,” Evans said. “You know, one time, two times, and then I think it is important to have some accountability, you know, a third time. Otherwise, there is no incentive to [say], okay, maybe I should think about this and engage in some way.”
Hurley had a different view on the program, saying it will exacerbate current issues at the Seattle Municipal Court.

“They're going to be asking for aggravated jail sentences for low-level property offenses,” Hurley said. “Almost all of those folks are experiencing homelessness and/or behavioral health disorders, and it's going to be very expensive for the City. If judges were to impose these jail sentences, it's going to make it less likely that we'll be able to resolve cases and will likely result in more trials as we vindicate our clients' rights, and will make it so that we don't actually address the underlying needs people have. You're going to pay a lot of money for a system to try to punish folks whose basic needs aren't being met.”

According to the press release about the program, “this approach lets prosecutors dynamically target patterns of individual behavior, rather than relying on a static list of names.” The reference to a list is a clear recall to Davison’s High Utilizers Initiative , which was in fact a list of frequent offenders with more than 12 misdemeanor referrals in five years. An investigation by PubliCola in 2022 showed that most of the people on this list were unhoused and many were suffering from major behavioral conditions, with almost half ordered to undergo a competency evaluation.
Evans said anyone with a major behavioral condition should be going through the mental health court and doesn’t think her program will have the same issues as the High Utilizers Initiative.
Hurley said that in some ways, the new HiPRO program is more expansive than Davison’s High Utilizers program due to its inclusion of shoplifting and car prowling.

“I was exceedingly surprised to see a theft related to someone who previously received a trespass notice be considered a HiPRO individual,” Hurley said. “That is a low-level behavior involving a nonviolent property offense, which almost always has no actual loss to the store.”
The CAO will be adding the ability to track the HiPRO cases to its data management system , although it is not clear when this new capability will be operational.
Evans emphasized that CAO attorneys will have complete discretion around decisions about eligibility for Connection Court and which cases to include in the HiPRO program.
But Hurley said it’s important to design systems with policies that make sense for the majority of cases coming through that system.

“It's hard for me to imagine in my mind a case that would not be appropriate for Connection Court where a person is charged with a low-level shoplift involving a business, including a trespass,” Hurley said. “And if you're going to rely on individual prosecutors, line prosecutors, to make decisions, it's going to invite bias. It's going to invite unequal decision making, and it's going to result in far more people being excluded from these pathways than we saw under the previous iteration of Connection Court.”

articles.title: Seattle's 'Centers & Corridors' Zoning Update Delayed Another Year
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The next phase of zoning changes planned to implement Seattle's twenty-year housing and job growth plan are on track to be delayed another year, according to a city briefing provided last week to the city's planning commission. A holdover from the Bruce Harrell administration, the " Centers & Corridors " zoning update had been set to rezone thirty new "neighborhood centers" for denser development and allow larger apartment buildings directly along transit corridors, but legal appeals have kept final approval at bay.
It doesn't look like that trend is set to change any time soon.

The appeals that have been assailing the environmental review underlying Harrell's One Seattle Comprehensive Plan since last February asserted flaws that have allegedly led to understated impacts from future growth on stormwater runoff, tree canopy, and other issues. But last month, a ruling from the state's Growth Management Hearings Board failed to find any evidence for those claims, upholding the way that the plan's final Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) was conducted.
But the board did throw the city officials a curveball that they're still grappling with.

Rather than studying "maximum likely development" under a future zoning scenario, the ruling stated, Seattle's Office of Planning and Community Development (OPCD) was required to analyze "maximum possible development", a fact that ropes in a significant number of housing units that are unlikely to be built in the plan's twenty-year horizon. Readjusting to study that maximum possible development expands the scope of the EIS considerably, even as the ruling itself acknowledges that Seattle is unlikely to see all parcels develop before updating its Comprehensive Plan again.

While the city was given a year to go back and fill in that additional analysis, any new zoning changes stemming from the EIS won't be able to be approved by the city council until the hearings board gives its stamp of approval. The deadline to get that analysis updated is September 9, 2027, with a compliance hearing scheduled for later that fall.

But despite the fact that OPCD is opening the EIS back up to do more analysis, there are no plans to adjust the city's preferred growth plan, despite what the aims of the appellants who had challenged it may be.

"The decision and order from the board is narrowly focused on the analysis in the EIS and what was, in their view, required to be in that analysis," Michael Hubner, OPCD's Long Range Planning Manager, told the planning commission last week. "We're certainly not bringing forward a new Comp Plan proposal, or any amendments to the plan based on this decision. And what's important is that the board did not order us to do so. The board did examine the Comprehensive Plan with respect to the issues raised in the appeal, and the city prevailed."

Hubner, who has been the planner sent to face community groups angry about seeing zoning changes brought to their neighborhoods, described the update that the city is required to make as a technical one.

"I think of it as really a technical add-in to our existing EIS, rather than changing anything fundamental about how we're planning for the next 20 years related to concurrent infrastructure investments, parks, all the things that the Comprehensive Plan addresses," Hubner said.

There are still a lot of outstanding questions that remain to be answered in the months ahead, including whether this additional required EIS work will impact Mayor Katie Wilson's attempt to go even further than the One Seattle plan when it comes to allowing additional density across Seattle's neighborhoods. Referred to as the "Taller, Denser, Faster" plan , Wilson's initial proposal has faced even more local opposition than Harrell's plan, but city planners had laid out a schedule that included potential adoption as soon as late 2027 – a schedule that now looks to be in doubt.
Could the city wrap up work on redoing the EIS well before the September deadline? Hubner described that as being unlikely.

"It's a pretty heavy lift to essentially add that information to the Comprehensive Plan EIS," Hubner said. "There's a lot of moving pieces there, so it's good we have a year, and we're starting to look at what it will take to update our analysis to meet the expectations of the board."

Updating the EIS to include these additional potential units would be a big enough lift for OPCD, but the hearings board appeal isn't the only challenge to the One Seattle Plan still alive. The same day that Hubner provided his update to the planning commission, Seattle's hearing examiner held a conference to discuss a set of city-level appeals that continue to advance on a parallel track.

Filed by Seattle symphony performer Jennifer Godfrey (who also filed the growth hearings board appeal) and Mount Baker lawyer John M. Cary, those two appeals have been trying to stop the One Seattle Plan in its tracks since last February. But changes in state law relating to exemptions under the State Environmental Policy Act (SEPA) caused the hearing examiner to dismiss both challenges, a dismissal that was ultimately reversed after further appeal to the state's Court of Appeals. That ruling seemed to affirm a major loophole in SEPA exemptions that applies to environmental review that hasn't yet been acted upon by a legislative body.

But there's another twist. Though the hearing examiner's office now has the appeal back in front of them, they may be forced to dismiss it again, following the approval of a bill approved this summer by the Seattle City Council that removed the path of city-level SEPA appeals for area-wide rezones and Comprehensive Plan amendments. Proposed by land use committee chair Eddie Lin, the bill proved very divisive and passed on a 5-4 vote , despite the fact that other jurisdictions including Bellevue, Tacoma and King County do not allow this path of city-level appeal.

Though it was initially unclear if that new law would apply retroactively to appeals that were already active, the hearing examiner has already dismissed another appeal on the grounds that the office now lacks jurisdiction, a challenge to the city's plans to keep housing prohibited in the Stadium District . While that suggests dismissal could occur here as well, the examiner hasn't yet ruled on that question.

"One of two potential things could happen: the hearing examiner will grant that motion and dismiss, and be appealed, or the hearing examiner will hear the appeal on its merits again over the next number of months," Hubner said. "We're looking at a calendar for the case that stretches into early next year potentially."

The exact schedule for those two appeals would likely be a bigger deal if OPCD wasn't already scrambling to address the Growth Management Hearings Board ruling. But a hearing on the merits, should they reach that stage, could potentially force additional changes to the EIS on top of those, extending the process even further.

While all of those legal issues continue to play out, Seattle's zoning framework – where midrise affordable housing projects are only legal to build on 3% of the city's land – will stay in place indefinitely.

articles.title: Columbia City Will Be Home to a Native-Owned Birth Center: Q&A With Camie Goldhammer
paras: In 2028, Columbia City will be home to a birth center owned by the Native community. Hummingbird Indigenous Family Services (Hummingbird), located on South Hudson Street in the neighborhood, recently bought the former Seattle Home Maternity birth center space, just a few blocks away on South Ferdinand Street. Seattle's Equitable Development Initiative gave close to $2.2 million to Hummingbird to support its purchase of the birth center and renovations.

In Washington State, Indigenous maternal mortality rates are more than seven times higher than rates for white mothers. The majority of these cases are preventable through better access to culturally responsive medical care and support services. Hummingbird offers culturally congruent support and care for Indigenous moms. The organization is also piloting a no-strings-attached guaranteed basic income project , offering a group of Indigenous mothers financial support from pregnancy until their baby's third year.

The Emerald spoke with Hummingbird's founding executive director Camie Goldhammer (Sisíthuŋwaŋ-Waȟpéthuŋwaŋ Oyáte) about the organization. Goldhammer is also a licensed clinical social worker and an internationally board-certified lactation consultant and full-spectrum Indigenous doula.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
YK: Tell me about what has influenced your approach to your work with Indigenous mothers.

CG: I describe myself as a suburban Indian. I grew up in Issaquah. My dad is my Native parent. My mom is non-Native. I was very close to my dad as well as my [paternal] grandma. My grandma taught me a lot about what it means to be a Dakota woman, to care for people and to learn about culture and our background. There were a lot of challenges too, because colonization impacted Native people for generations. Many people in my family went to boarding school, which resulted in varying degrees of cultural disconnection.

My Indigenous activism started in high school. Our high school mascot was the Issaquah High School Indians, and I worked on changing that. In my junior year, the football team had an impromptu pep rally. They cut down a 300-year-old [Indigenous] story pole in Beaver Lake Park, set it on fire, peed on it, and all the things. This fueled me to fight. I always felt strongly about serving my Native community.

When I became a mom almost 18 years ago, breastfeeding was a formative experience for me. When I breastfed my daughter for the first time, I recognized that a healthy attachment between a Native mom and her Native babies is the antidote to colonization. That's when I went full force into supporting Native moms when they're pregnant and caring for young children.
YK: Could you tell me more about this concept of breastfeeding as an antidote to colonization?

CG: Culture is typically our food, our spirituality, our language, and our connection to land. Learning this is almost always through the mother, especially in the early years. When we look at colonization and the methods used to try to destroy us, there were a lot of attacks on mothering, like separating children from their mothers and their teachings. It's about cutting the attachment to a mom, which destabilizes the child's sense of security. Colonization created unhealthy attachments. It promoted fierce independence and a lack of security, which increases fear and [the perspective of] scarcity.

My favorite definition of security is the belief that when bad things happen, good things will follow. For many of us, the good thing that followed was the thing that mom did, like you fall and skin your knee. It hurts. We can't prevent those hard things from happening, but it's the hugs, the loves, and the “Are you okay?” that are formative. A lot of times we focus on the health of the children, but in my opinion, the best thing to do for the children is to take care of their mothers.
YK: Tell me about Hummingbird's guaranteed basic income program.

CG: It's called the Nest, and it's a pilot program. We've been funded to provide a guaranteed basic income to 150 Indigenous moms. They enter the program sometime in their second or third trimester, and they receive $1,250 per month, no strings attached, through their child's third birthday. It comes to a little over $45,000 over the course of three years, plus however long they were pregnant. At the child's third year, we open a $5,000 529 college savings account for the child as our investment into the next generation. We started enrolling 15 moms a month in August of 2023. Our first baby turned 3 in July. Our last baby turns 3 in October 2027. Each month, kids turning 3 come in for their exit celebration.

All of the families have access to Hummingbird's culturally congruent wraparound services if they want them. We've found that most people in the Nest engage in services and that's where we've seen the greatest impact.

CG: We have a maternal mortality rate of zero. We believe that the combination of our services can eliminate the maternal mortality crisis. We've seen very low prematurity rates and less hypertension. They experience more financial, housing, and food security. Maternal mood disorders are reduced. There are higher breastfeeding rates, which promote a stronger attachment and connection with their babies. Almost all the moms in the Nest took time off after they had their babies to bond and recover. That's something many families are unable to do.

I also met a Nest mom and dad at their baby's exit celebration, and I asked if they were worried about not having the monthly income anymore. The dad told me that because his wife was in the Nest program, he didn't have to hustle for a second and a third job to make ends meet. With that ease, he was able to join a union apprentice-training program. He said he was graduating to a journeyman job the following month, which would bring in more income than the Nest program.
YK: I heard Hummingbird has a research and evaluations department that's referred to as "data sovereignty." What does data sovereignty mean?

CG: Data sovereignty came out of the idea that we need to protect data about ourselves in the same way that we need to protect our land and our bodies. When evaluations or studies are done [about Indigenous communities] the outcomes almost always live at large institutions and universities that are not managed by Native people. We should be answering questions that our community is asking, not what a professor somewhere else is probing. We have a team of five Indigenous researchers and evaluators and we publish articles.

We evaluate our own services, and we're working on other research too, like an Indigenous, perinatal, mood-disorder screening tool. The two tools most used now are not great at screening perinatal mood disorders in people of color. We want to create a tool that will work for Native moms. We find that so many are suffering in silence. We're also conducting a large, national, reproductive justice landscape review for the Native community.
YK: Tell me about other Hummingbird programs.
CG: We have home visit programs. All of them are community-designed and voluntary. The visits are driven by what the family wants and are meant to meet the family's goals.

We have doula home visits during pregnancy and up to three months post-partum. We also have Pilimakua home visits, which start as early as 27 weeks into pregnancy and up to the baby's third birthday. ["Pili" is the 'Ōlelo Hawai'i word for "connection." "Makua" is the Kānaka Maoli tradition of generational caregiving.] These visits center around three pillars: understanding infant and child development; caregiver mindfulness and self-compassion; and culture and language reclamation.

An example of a visit could be that a family heard from their pediatrician that their child should start solid foods at 6 months. The Hummingbird team might share information about what to watch for in the child's development progress, which can show the baby's ready, like a pincer grip to hold food and when they stop tongue thrust, which is their way of expelling solid food. For caregiver mindfulness, the mother can ask how solid food might affect the relationship between mother and baby. With language and culture reclamation, the home visit might include a conversation about looking up what your people have given for the first food, because cultures throughout the world often have a first-food ceremony.

We also have the Indigenous emotional wellness program for moms who are experiencing perinatal mood disorders. Our two peer counselors in the program offer non-clinical support. Another title for them is "Indigenous Emotional Bestie." They're meant to offer help in conjunction with a therapist or a clinician and other services at Hummingbird.
YK: Tell me about the importance of the birth center for the community.

CG: We need alternative birth spaces. We have many families that are just not cared for properly at hospitals and choose a birth center for many different reasons, including comfort level, proximity to a hospital, and living situations.

We're excited about the birth center. The building was home to Seattle Home Maternity Service. The founders, Suzy Myers and Marge Mansfield, purchased it in the late 1970s, and they ran the Seattle Midwifery School out of its basement before it became a licensed birth center in 1983. Thousands of babies have been loved and cared for there together with their moms. It has good energy and good medicine in it.

articles.title: The Roundup: Why Would We Replace Route 7?
paras: When I was growing up, I had the key to the city.

Anywhere I needed to go, the 7 had my back. I remember when a ride cost less than a dollar. Basketball practice, teen dances at Rainier Vista Boys & Girls Club, Teen Late Night — back when you could run a few games at Rainier Community Center, then hop the 7 and get games in at Rainier Beach.
Then I grew up. My first job was at NikeTown downtown. Guess which bus I used to get there? That's right, the 7.
And it's not just me. The 7 is the second-most-used bus route in King County.

When I learned from Emerald contributor Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero that there were plans on the table to end Route 7 in favor of a RapidRide line in 2032 , I was confused. Who would this serve? Who asked for this?
The proposal would eliminate over 20 stops — in the South End — and would make the bus come less frequently.

My mind goes to the seniors, the students, the workers in our community who are not simply commuting downtown, but using transit to get to places within the neighborhood. How can that happen if 20 stops disappear? Are the elderly or differently abled folks supposed to walk a mile to access a bus stop?
The 7 is more than a bus line; for many in our community, it's a lifeline.

This week, I spoke with Jacquelyn about this proposal. She went on a ride-along on the 7 , with elected officials and community members, to see the stops that would be eliminated and speak with some of the South Enders who would be impacted.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
MD: You've been following this proposal to replace the 7. Can you briefly tell us what has happened and where we are in the process?

JJR: The proposal essentially has the goal of making buses faster and more reliable, and comes from King County's intention to improve bus services overall. So RapidRides are becoming more and more popular in King County. The South Seattle RapidRide line was proposed in 2019 and delayed due to the pandemic. The project picked back up in August. King County Metro is working to present it to the King County Council. So, essentially, they're going to go to the Council and present what's called an alignment ordinance, and they're briefing the Council on the most updated project that they have. It'll also be an opportunity for community members to go to King County Council and share their thoughts on what they think about the project, and there could potentially be a vote in November about whether King County Council actually fully approves this project or not.
MD: I heard the RapidRide line does two things simultaneously — runs less frequently than the 7 and has 20 less stops. This true? If so, how can Metro call this more efficient?

JJR: Yes. I think that's the question that a lot of community members have. I think that's the big question on whether this project actually makes sense for the South End, and community members certainly don't think so. I think these are part of the concerns that community members and advocacy organizations are bringing up to the Council. Everyone appreciates the investment, but they're not sure it makes sense.
MD: I saw the video of you on this ride-along. Can you tell me who organized it, who attended, and what you learned from community members?

JJR: It was organized by the Nondrivers Alliance and the Transit Riders Union. Community members showed up, like people who ride the bus, leaders from a few community organizations, and a few current and potential politicians. Rebecca Saldaña and Toshiko Hasegawa came; they're candidates for the King County Council seat that represents the South End. Kelabe Tewolde was there; he's running for the 37th Legislative District, the House seat. And then City Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck [was there].

I personally got to see which stops could potentially be eliminated, and I think for people who don't take the bus a lot, it's hard to imagine how long of a distance the potential stops could be. For someone who has a disability or is older, or even a family who has a stroller, walking those longer distances can be really challenging, especially along Rainier Avenue, because there are a lot of infrastructure improvements that need to happen. The sidewalks are uneven, and it can really be hard for a lot of people to navigate.

A lot of what I'm hearing from people is that they're confused about this proposal. It's a very important line, and even aside from the nostalgia aspect, it's the second-most-used bus line in the entire county. Over 11,000 people use it every day. So people were confused about why this was happening.
MD: Why can't we have the RapidRide line and the traditional 7? Why is this an either-or situation?

JJR: That is a question a lot people have for the Executive and the Council. Why can't we have both? A lot of people mentioned the importance of the 7 in terms of navigating Rainier Valley and getting to important places, like grocery stores, pharmacies, and businesses. A lot of people use it in the South End without going downtown.
Budget season is here. Proposals are being presented. And the community is coming out in full force for input.
Developers want to axe a beloved weeping willow tree on South Brandon Street. Neighbors say “No way.” Can we have housing density and trees?
Is the U.S. government complicit in the war in Gaza? On Oct. 10, organizers from around the country will meet in Seattle for a tribunal to determine the answer.
Businesses in Rainier Beach are focused on two things: safety and service.
On Oct. 10, the Emerald will host a forum to introduce the community to the two candidates looking to represent the South End on the King County Council.

This is an abbreviated version of The Roundup newsletter. To get the entire newsletter, including a weekly list of events to check out and my shout-out to South End Gems, subscribe here . See you next week!

Mike Davis is the newsletter editor and Voices editor at the South Seattle Emerald. Born and raised in Seattle's South End, Mike is a longtime journalist who's covered everything from arts and culture to sports to politics.

Editor's Note: This article was updated on Oct. 14 to clarify that Metro is in the process of presenting a plan to the King County Council. The council's Transportation, Economy, and Environment Committee will hear a presentation about a potential RapidRide R line on Oct. 20.

articles.title: Duplicative services and commuter route truncation, again
articles.author: Sherwin Lee
paras: We’re about a month into the Fall shakeup, where a substantial number of service changes were implemented to improve connections to Link. This is a recurring playbook that Metro has used ever since light rail service began: identify duplicative services and restructure existing bus routes to connect to Link stations rather than running all the way into downtown Seattle.

When Northgate Link opened, Sound Transit truncated many of its 510 series routes to connect at Link instead. After Lynnwood Link, all of Community Transit’s direct services to downtown Seattle were restructured . And with the August changes , both Metro and Sound Transit no longer offer any one-seat rides from Bellevue or Issaquah to Seattle, save for the 2 Line.

Critics of this approach generally lament the loss of the one-seat ride, that trip times generally increase when factoring in wait times, and that Link is not necessarily faster point-to-point than express routes. The Sound Transit subreddit and other various community forums feature countless examples of riders testifying to that end. There is even now a “Restore 554” petition circulating among Issaquah residents, urging the restoration of a direct Issaquah-Seattle route.

The planning justifications for this type of restructuring are quite straightforward: Link provides a frequent high-capacity serve to major regional centers; instead of running costly peak-directional bus service, reinvest the hours into boosting local connecting service. This implementation aligns with Jarrett Walker’s “frequency is freedom” mantra and is generally a position this blog has supported.

In practice, however, real-world conditions can muddy the picture. Take, for example, the 554’s successor: the 556, which now provides frequent all-day service between Issaquah and Bellevue. Those previously using the 554 (or the 550 local stops along Bellevue Way) to get to Seattle must now connect at South Bellevue Station for the same trip.

These transfer conditions can greatly deteriorate due to local northbound congestion on Bellevue Way just in the short span between the I-90 off-ramp and the station bus stops. Riders agonizingly wait for traffic to crawl up Bellevue Way only to see Seattle-bound trains glide past over their heads. Even in the southbound direction, buses have to yield to northbound traffic in order to turn into the station bays, which adds travel time variability.
The physical infrastructure in between the connecting services is important too. Jarrett Walker touches on this point in one of his foundational articles on transferring:

… the unpleasantness of the connection experience depends on many details of how the connection works. If two buses or trains arrive on opposite sides of a platform, facing one another five meters apart, with their doors open at the same time, walking out of one and into the other is a pretty low level of inconvenience for most passengers. If the connection involves getting off a bus, crossing a busy street, and waiting for another bus not knowing when it will arrive, the inconvenience is much greater.

As it were, the connecting infrastructure at South Bellevue and Mercer Island stations is less than ideal. Both settings require a moderate walk (across a signalized intersection in the latter case, largely thanks to Mercer Island’s opposition to an 80th Ave transfer point) and ascending or descending to the train platform. This can add a lot of variability, particularly for those with limited mobility, on top of the wait for the connecting service.

Negative feedback is often amplified over positive feedback, as human beings are far more likely to complain about things that hurt them rather than praise the things that help them. But in many ways, what is often seen as a degradation in one part of the network typically means an improvement in another part.

554 riders, for example, might glowingly reminisce about the quick travel times across I-90, but forget about the frequent outbound reliability issues inflicted by 2nd Avenue congestion (as I so often personally experienced). And although not quite a zero sum game, the changes have meant a substantially better commute for Issaquah-Bellevue riders, among other parts of the system.

Big restructures in the regional network will invariably result in system-wide tradeoffs, but that doesn’t mean agencies’ hands are tied. Barring a miraculous way of sending buses congestion-free right up (or down) to the Link platforms, transfer penalties can be offset by improving frequency and reliability across all segments.

Making the 556 a frequent all-day route that connects to frequent 2 Line service is certainly an excellent start, but continued work on reliability improvements are always in order. This might mean more attentive maintenance to ensure fewer breakdowns of Link trains. Or it could mean stronger partnerships with WSDOT and local jurisdictions to give signal or lane priority to buses.

Whatever the solution, transit agencies cannot go it alone here. Route 8’s dramatic reliability leaps were only possible by some repainting (and other minor infrastructural improvements) from SDOT. In the same way, local jurisdictions owe it to the taxpaying public to squeeze out the full return on our massive regional investment in transit. Helping create reliable well-connected services is a small, but important step to get there.

articles.title: Ballard Link Community Forum on October 19
articles.author: Nathan Dickey
paras: Seattle City Councilmember (District 6) and Sound Transit Boardmember Dan Strauss is hosting a community form discussing the Ballard Link Extension alongside several other elected officials and Sound Transit representatives. The forum will be held in the Osberg Great Hall at the National Nordic Museum on Monday, October 19, from 6-8pm .

In a newsletter emailed to constituents last week, Dan Strauss announced the event while highlighting his efforts to get Sound Transit to commit to building the full Ballard Link Extension to Market Street. These included requiring Sound Transit staff to determine when the agency would be able to complete the Ballard Link Extension under current conditions, and looking for ways to reduce project costs in order to open the extension sooner. Currently, the agency expects to open the SODO to Seattle Center portion of the Ballard Link Extension in 2042.

In July, Sound Transit fulfilled Strauss’ first requirement with the announcement the rest of the project could be delayed to 2060 unless significant cost savings are found. When voters passed ST3 in 2016, the entire Ballard Link Extension was expected to open in 2035. In 2021, this schedule slipped to 2037 or 2039 as Sound Transit realized the cost to build a second Link-only tunnel under downtown and managing other complications would far exceed expectations . After calculating “bottom-up” cost estimates for the proposed design of the extension last year, the agency found the full project could cost nearly twice its previous estimate. Compounded with exploding cost estimates across ST3, the Sound Transit Board voted to defer construction of line past Seattle Center until costs were reduced or additional revenue were found.

Sound Transit says it may be able to open the full extension in 2042 if the agency can reduce the total estimated cost by $1 billion (or identify that much in new revenue), begin acquiring property by 2030, finish design by 2032, and lock in funding to start construction by 2033. Regardless, Ballard Link advocates remain dedicated to pushing Sound Transit to return to the originally promised date of opening in 2035.

At the community forum, Sound Transit is expected to share more about its proposed timeline for the Ballard Link Extension, the work agency staff have been doing to reduce costs, and its next steps for the project. There will also be a Q&A session.

Those interested in a seat should probably arrive early. The National Nordic Museum is located at the intersection of 28th Ave NW and NW Market Street, just under a mile west of the planned terminus of the Ballard Link Extension. Nearby bus stops are served by King County Metro Routes 17 and 44 .

paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. So, here’s a short list to get you started.

articles.title: The Restaurants and Bars With the Best Views in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Meg van Huygen</name>
paras: We’re not going to say people don’t come to Seattle for the food, but they definitely come for the views. The Cascades to the east, the Olympics to the west, Mount Rainier to the south, and water everywhere you look. Thanks to exceptional restaurants that occupy some choice real estate, enjoying a multiple-course meal or award-winning fare while drinking in the sights is a piece of cake.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: The 38 Best Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. Every place on the list has been open for at least six months, proving its merit.

Like many menus, this map updates every quarter — removal from the Eater 38 doesn’t mean a restaurant isn’t still awesome and won’t return in the future. New to the map as of August 2026: unassuming neighborhood gem Three Sacks Full; seafood-focused French bistro L’Oursin; and La Cabaña, where you can find some of the city’s best pupusas.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
